content: Most surgical procedures require an incision in the skin to provide access to the surgical site. At the conclusion of these procedures, the wounds are typically closed completely. The skin, being the outermost layer of the body, is underlain by subcutaneous tissue, which is composed of loose connective tissue and fat. There is ongoing debate regarding whether the subcutaneous tissue should be closed during wound closure. Some surgeons argue that closing the subcutaneous tissue reduces dead space and decreases the risk of wound complications. Others believe that this step is unnecessary, as it prolongs the operation and requires additional suture material without providing clear benefits. The objective of this review was to compare the advantages, such as reduced wound-related complications, and disadvantages, such as increased operative time, of subcutaneous closure versus no subcutaneous closure in patients undergoing non-caesarean surgical procedures. A comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted in August 2013, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. No restrictions were placed on language, publication date, or study setting. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing subcutaneous closure with no subcutaneous closure were included, regardless of the type of suture material or suture technique (continuous or interrupted). All RCTs were included in the analysis, irrespective of language, publication status, year of publication, or sample size. Two independent reviewers identified eligible trials and extracted data. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for binary outcomes, while mean differences (MD) with 95% CI were calculated for continuous outcomes. Meta-analyses were performed using both fixed-effect and random-effects models, and intention-to-treat analyses were conducted whenever possible. Eight RCTs met the inclusion criteria, with six trials providing data for the review. All six trials were deemed to have a high risk of bias. These trials included a total of 815 participants, with 410 assigned to subcutaneous closure and 405 to no subcutaneous closure. Among all participants, 7.7% (63/815) developed superficial surgical site infections. There was no clear evidence of a difference in infection rates between the two groups (RR 0.84; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.33; very low-quality evidence). Superficial wound dehiscence was reported in only two trials, affecting 7.9% (17/215) of participants. It remains unclear whether the absence of this outcome in other trials was due to a lack of occurrence or failure to measure it. Among the trials that reported this outcome, there was no clear evidence of a difference between the groups (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.22 to 1.41; very low-quality evidence). Deep wound dehiscence was reported in only one trial, occurring in 8.3% (5/60) of participants. Again, there was no clear evidence of a difference between the groups (RR 0.25; 95% CI 0.03 to 2.11; very low-quality evidence). Three trials assessed the length of hospital stay and found no significant difference between the groups (MD 0.10 days; 95% CI -0.45 to 0.64; very low-quality evidence). It is unclear whether these findings reflect a true lack of effect or simply a lack of evidence. The wide confidence intervals suggest that significant benefits or harms from subcutaneous closure cannot be ruled out. None of the included trials evaluated the impact of subcutaneous closure on quality of life, long-term patient outcomes (follow-up periods ranged from one week to two months), or the financial implications for healthcare providers. In conclusion, the current evidence is of very low quality and is insufficient to either support or refute the use of subcutaneous closure in non-caesarean surgical procedures. Subcutaneous closure may influence patient outcomes and healthcare resource utilization, but further well-designed trials with low risk of bias are needed to provide more definitive evidence.
